# Results: bus delay analytics and delay prediction on Boston MBTA data (PySpark)

*Generated by `src/make_docs.py`. Every number comes from files in `outputs/`. Data: MBTA "Bus Arrival Departure Times 2024" (calendar year 2024; months Jan, Apr, Jul, Oct), real scheduled and actual times.*

## 1. Data and completeness
9,108,352 raw events -> **4,606,471** kept (50.57%). Events with no actual time were dropped (data-collection gaps), and only 'Schedule'-standard trips are judged on delay
(the dataset says 'Headway'-standard trips must be judged on headways instead). Full waterfall: `outputs/tables/delay_waterfall.csv`, figure `fig4_completeness_waterfall.png`.

| stage | rows_in | rows_out | pct_retained |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. raw arrival/departure rows | 9108352 | 9108352 | 100.0 |
| 2. drop null service_date/route/trip/order | 9108352 | 9108169 | 99.998 |
| 3. drop duplicate (date, trip, timepoint order) | 9108169 | 9108137 | 99.9996 |
| 4. drop rows without a valid scheduled time | 9108137 | 9108137 | 100.0 |
| 5. drop rows without an actual time | 9108137 | 8425094 | 92.5007 |
| 6. drop |delay| > 7200 s | 8425094 | 8424946 | 99.9982 |
| 7. keep schedule-standard trips | 8424946 | 4606471 | 54.6766 |

## 2. How late are buses?
Delay = actual minus scheduled departure at a timepoint. Over 4,606,471 events: mean **4.3 min**, median 3.0 min, 90th percentile 11.7 min.
**On time** (between -1 and +5 min) = **55.4%**; late (> 5 min) 34.1%; early 10.6%.

- By hour, the lowest on-time share is at 22h (48.4%) and the highest at 5h (67.6%). Overnight hours have fewer trips.
- Weekday mean delay: peak 4.4 min vs off-peak 4.2 min; weekend: peak 4.4 vs off-peak 4.7 min (peak = 07-10h and 17-20h scheduled hour).
- Delay by position in the trip (first 15 timepoints): 2.5 min at timepoint 1, a maximum of 5.0 min at timepoint 6, then 1.2 min at timepoint 14. The pattern is not monotonic, and later timepoints cover far fewer trips, so it is not a pure "delay accumulates" curve. By point type: start 2.5 min, middle 4.9 min, end 3.2 min.

Five most delayed routes (at least 100 events; `delay_by_route.csv`):

| route_id | n | mean_delay_sec | p90_delay_sec | on_time_rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 29 | 32612 | 510.96 | 1246 | 0.37 |
| CT2 | 46063 | 465.1 | 1037 | 0.37 |
| 47 | 69118 | 448.81 | 1113 | 0.42 |
| 245 | 6611 | 446.38 | 949 | 0.38 |
| 556 | 3774 | 402.13 | 945 | 0.47 |

## 3. Actual vs scheduled run time
Between consecutive timepoints the mean scheduled run time is 315 s and the mean actual run time 323 s (on average 8.8 s added per hop; 3,882,783 hops).
Over 1,442 segments with enough peak and off-peak events, the median **actual** peak/off-peak slowdown ratio is **1.039** and the median **scheduled** ratio 1.036
(correlation between the two across segments: 0.39). 12.7% of segments have a scheduled ratio within 1% of 1.0, i.e. the timetable plans the same run time at peak and off-peak.

## 4. Headway (bunching) on high-frequency routes
On 3,515,157 headway-standard events the mean ratio of actual to scheduled gap is 1.014; **17.2%** of gaps are under half the scheduled gap (bunching) and **14.6%** are over 1.5x (large gaps).

## 5. Delay prediction (Spark MLlib)
**Task.** At the moment a bus leaves its previous timepoint, predict its delay at the next one: (a) delay in minutes (regression) and (b) late = more than 5 min (classification).
Only 'Schedule'-standard trips are used.

**Split (temporal, no leakage).** In each month the last 25% of the days are held out. Train: 3,379,953 events on 91 days (2024-01-01 to 2024-10-23); the models are fitted on a
seeded sample of 1,001,114 of them (cap 1,000,000, so local-mode training stays in minutes). Test: **1,226,518** events on 32 days. All metrics below are on the test days only.

**Features** (all known before the event): route_id_idx, direction_id_idx, point_type_idx, hour_of_day, day_of_week, month, time_point_order, route_hist_mean_delay_min, route_hist_late_rate, rtp_hist_mean_delay_min, prev_delay_min, has_prev. `route_hist_*` and `rtp_hist_*` are route and route+timepoint averages computed on the training days only and broadcast-joined;
`prev_delay_min` is the delay at the previous timepoint of the same trip (a `lag` window over earlier stops only). Model: gradient-boosted trees (`GBTRegressor`, `GBTClassifier`), 40 rounds, depth 5, seed 42.
The second model leaves out the previous-delay features to show how much they matter.

### Regression: delay in minutes
| model | RMSE (min) | MAE (min) | R2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline: train mean | 6.477 | 4.427 | -0.002 |
| baseline: previous delay carried forward | 3.327 | 2.055 | 0.736 |
| GBT without previous delay | 5.798 | 3.892 | 0.197 |
| GBT (full features) | 2.921 | 1.643 | 0.796 |

### Classification: late or not
| model | accuracy | precision | recall | F1 | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline: never late | 0.646 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | n/a |
| baseline: previous delay carried forward | 0.875 | 0.879 | 0.750 | 0.809 | 0.921 |
| GBT without previous delay | 0.704 | 0.657 | 0.343 | 0.451 | 0.734 |
| GBT (full features) | 0.894 | 0.914 | 0.774 | 0.838 | 0.946 |

- **Regression.** On held-out days the full GBT has MAE 1.64 min and R2 0.80, against MAE 4.43 min for predicting the training mean and 2.05 min for carrying the previous delay forward (20.1% lower MAE than the better baseline). The model is clearly better than the best simple baseline.
- **Where the skill comes from.** Without the previous-timepoint delay the GBT's MAE is 3.89 min (12.1% below the mean baseline), so schedule-only information (hour, weekday, route, timepoint) explains some of the delay; the previous delay adds the rest.
- **Classification (late = more than 5 min).** Full GBT: accuracy 89.4%, precision 91.4%, recall 77.4%, F1 0.838, AUC 0.946. Late rate in the test days is 35.4%, so accuracy alone is not informative; the carried-forward baseline reaches AUC 0.921 and without the previous delay the GBT reaches AUC 0.734.

**Most used features** (full GBT): regression: previous-timepoint delay (0.70), route (0.13), route+timepoint avg delay (train) (0.04), point type (0.04); classification: previous-timepoint delay (0.73), route (0.11), timepoint order (0.05), has previous timepoint (0.03). Importance shows what the trees split on, not what causes delay.

Fit times on 4 cores: regressor 30.5 s, classifier 36.3 s (data preparation 14.7 s). Figures: `fig5_ml_regression.png`, `fig6_ml_classification.png`, `fig7_ml_feature_importance.png`.

**Reading this honestly.** The predictions are 'next-timepoint' forecasts, made when the bus leaves the previous timepoint, not day-ahead forecasts. The model is evaluated on later days of the same four months; it says nothing about other months, years or other cities.

## 6. Performance (machine: Apple M3, 8 logical cores = 4 performance + 4 efficiency, 16.0 GB RAM; Spark 3.5.3, openjdk version "17.0.21" 2026-10-20, Python 3.11.13)
Baseline: Spark `local[1]`. Each core count ran in its own process; `shuffle.partitions`=8; adaptive execution off; no caching between runs. Stage times each include their Parquet read and write (needed to force execution). Speedup S_N = T1 / TN on median total time.

| cores | clean s | window+agg s | total median s | min-max s | throughput rows/s | speedup S_N | efficiency | oversubscribed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 167.6 | 50.1 | 217.7 | 217.7 - 217.7 | 38,699 | 1.00 | 1.00 | False |
| 2 | 84.5 | 29.8 | 114.3 | 114.3 - 114.3 | 73,735 | 1.91 | 0.95 | False |
| 4 | 53.5 | 24.3 | 77.9 | 77.9 - 77.9 | 108,212 | 2.80 | 0.70 | False |

8,424,946 cleaned events; 1 timed runs after 0 discarded warm-up per core count; 6g driver heap. Per-stage speedup: 1 cores: clean 1.00, window_agg 1.00; 2 cores: clean 1.98, window_agg 1.68; 4 cores: clean 3.13, window_agg 2.06.

### Model training (features + GBT regressor + GBT classifier)

| cores | features s | fit regressor s | fit classifier s | total median s | speedup S_N | efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 25.9 | 48.7 | 49.3 | 123.9 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 2 | 17.3 | 29.4 | 29.0 | 75.7 | 1.64 | 0.82 |
| 4 | 14.1 | 20.0 | 18.7 | 52.8 | 2.35 | 0.59 |

1,001,114 training rows, 40 rounds, depth 5; 1 timed run(s) after 0 discarded warm-up.

### Broadcast vs shuffle join (local[4])

| join variant | median s | min-max s | shuffle write bytes (median/run) | plan file |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| broadcast | 1.726 | 1.726 - 1.726 | 147,185 | outputs/explain_join_broadcast.txt |
| shuffle | 2.936 | 2.936 - 2.936 | 134,376,215 | outputs/explain_join_shuffle.txt |

Joining the train-only route / route+timepoint history tables onto the test events. Broadcast = `F.broadcast()` hint on the small history tables. Shuffle = no hint and `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold=-1`, giving sort-merge joins with `Exchange` nodes (see the saved plans). Adaptive query execution is off so Spark cannot silently switch strategy. Shuffle bytes come from the Spark event log; broadcast data movement is not counted as shuffle.

**Reading.** 1 cores: S=1.00 (efficiency 1.00), 2 cores: S=1.91 (efficiency 0.95), 4 cores: S=2.80 (efficiency 0.70). Speedup is sub-linear: some work is serial (JVM start-up, CSV parsing coordination, driver-side `toPandas`, shuffles), and this chip has 4 efficiency cores besides 4 performance cores, which may also lower efficiency at higher N (not isolated in these measurements).

## 7. Correctness
PASS: 14,458 events on 6 routes recomputed in pandas directly from the raw CSV matched Spark (max abs diff in mean/std/on-time 6.8e-13). Tests: `tests/test_delay.py` (cleaning rules, midnight wrap, pandas cross-check) and `tests/test_delay_model.py` (no leakage in the lag feature, temporal split, history from training rows only, metrics).

## 8. Comparison with the base paper
Base paper as cited in our proposal: N. L. Mnyone and N. U. Amin (2026), *Real-Time Data Processing in Smart Transportation Using Apache Spark*, Preprints, DOI 10.20944/preprints202603.1261.v1.
**The team must confirm every statement about the paper from the paper itself; this project did not read it.** According to the proposal, the paper used synthetic GPS/vehicle-sensor logs, Spark Core RDDs and basic Spark SQL, and studied ingestion bottlenecks and memory use on single-table feeds. Contrast of *methodology only* (no numeric comparison):

| Aspect | Base paper (as stated in our proposal) | This project |
|---|---|---|
| Data | synthetic GPS / sensor logs | real scheduled and actual bus events (Boston MBTA, 9,108,352 rows) |
| API | RDDs, basic Spark SQL | DataFrames, `Window` functions (lag per trip), Spark MLlib |
| Analytics | ingestion bottlenecks, memory | delay, on-time and bunching metrics, delay prediction with baselines and a held-out test |
| Join/shuffle | not part of our summary | measured broadcast vs sort-merge join with plans and shuffle bytes |
| Scaling | memory / ingestion | speedup, latency and efficiency of the pipeline and of model training on 1/2/4 cores |

## 9. Limitations
1. **Boston only.** Results describe the MBTA bus network in 2024, not any other city.
2. **Timepoints only.** Only timepoints (not every stop) and only departures are recorded; delay is departure delay at timepoints.
3. **Data gaps.** 'Actual' times come from MBTA's own vehicle tracking; the dataset notes data is not guaranteed complete, and 7.5% of events had no actual time.
4. **Four sampled months** (one per season) of 2024, not the full year; no claim about other months.
5. **Schedule-standard trips only.** 'Headway'-standard trips are not judged on schedule delay and are not in the model.
6. **Prediction scope.** Next-timepoint prediction using the previous timepoint's delay; the model is evaluated on later days of the same months and trained on a sample of the training days (cap in `config.yaml`).
7. **Straight comparison with simple baselines** is reported; where the model barely beats them the text above says so.
8. **Single machine.** Benchmarks run Spark in `local[N]` on one laptop with mixed performance/efficiency cores, so they are noisy and do not represent a cluster.
9. Peak is defined by scheduled hour (07-10h and 17-20h).
